stem: A plant has fixed costs of $120,000 per year. Each unit costs $18 to make and sells for $30. How many units per year must be sold to break even?
eli5: At the break-even point total revenue equals total cost. Each unit sold contributes (price - variable cost) toward the fixed costs, so the break-even quantity is fixed cost divided by that contribution margin.
solution:
Contribution per unit = 30 - 18 = $12.

Break-even quantity = \frac{120,000}{12} = 10,000 units per year.

solution:
Expected value of B = 0.70 × 70,000 + 0.30 × 0 = $49,000.

stem: A machine costs $60,000 and $4,000 per year to run, plus $2.50 for each unit it makes. It lasts 10 years with no salvage value. Buying the part instead costs $6.00 per unit. At 8% interest, how many units per year make owning the machine break even?
eli5: Put owning on an annual basis: the first cost times the capital recovery factor (A/P), plus the fixed annual cost, plus the unit cost times the quantity. Set that equal to the purchase price times the quantity and solve.
solution:
(A/P, 8%, 10) = 0.14903, so the annual cost of owning before any units = 60,000(0.14903) + 4,000 = $12,942.

Each unit made saves 6.00 - 2.50 = $3.50.

Break-even = \frac{12,942}{3.50} = 3,698 units per year.

stem: A facility costs $2,000,000 to build and $25,000 per year to maintain, forever. At 5% interest, what is its capitalized cost?
eli5: Capitalized cost is the present worth of something that lasts indefinitely. A perpetual annual cost A has a present worth of A / i, because that sum earns exactly A in interest each year.
terms: present worth
the amount today that is equivalent to money received or paid in the future, at a given interest rate

eli5: Expected value weights each outcome by its probability: the chance of winning times the profit, minus the chance of losing times the cost of the proposal.

stem: A venture gains $80,000 if it succeeds and loses $20,000 if it fails. At what probability of success is its expected value zero?
eli5: Set the expected value to zero: p × gain = (1 - p) × loss. Solving gives p = loss / (gain + loss). Above that probability the venture is worth taking on expected value alone.
